title: Discovery
summary: Discovery is the tactic that covers the internal reconnaissance an adversary performs after gaining a foothold, mapping users, systems, shares, permissions, security controls, and network topology so that the next move is informed. Behaviours include enumerating local and domain accounts, querying directory services, listing remote systems and open shares, scanning internal address space for live hosts and services, reading configuration and cloud metadata, and checking for the presence of security tooling. The volume of telemetry is deceptive: almost all of this activity is native to the platform, produces normal-looking events, and is generated constantly by legitimate administration, inventory, monitoring, and software deployment. Command line and script block logging capture many of the queries, but only if enabled and centrally collected, since local logs are easily lost. Authentication records reveal lateral enumeration through logon types and target patterns, while cloud audit logs show unusual describe, list, or permission-enumeration calls from a principal that has never made them before. Detecting Discovery in isolation is close to impossible because the primitives are not malicious. Progress depends on baselining which hosts and accounts normally run which discovery commands, scoring breadth over any single action, and correlating a burst of enumeration from one identity with the privileged access or lateral movement that follows it. High-fidelity signals are rare, so prioritisation must be ruthless.
objectives: Enumerate the main discovery behaviours across endpoint, directory, network, and cloud environments and the evidence each produces.
Explain why native enumeration activity cannot be detected with signature-style rules and what baseline data is required instead.
Score discovery by breadth and rarity, for example a single host issuing many distinct enumeration commands in a short window.
Use authentication and network flow telemetry to detect internal scanning and share enumeration that command line logs miss.
Correlate a discovery burst with the privilege escalation or lateral movement that follows to judge intent.
Design a hunting hypothesis for post-compromise discovery that can be run repeatedly with low analyst cost.
